items.explanation: Sugar was the payoff leg: grown by enslaved workers in the Americas, shipped to Europe, and sold for the profits that funded the whole cycle. The plantation image shows where that leg of the triangle began.
items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Triangular trade: 'three-way Atlantic commerce linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas in goods, enslaved people, and plantation products'

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Europe-to-Africa leg carried manufactured goods outward.
option_explanations.B: Right — plantation products sailed from the Americas to Europe.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the Africa-to-Americas leg carried enslaved people, not sugar.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the triangular trade was intercontinental by definition.

options: (A) The leg from Europe to Africa, carrying manufactured goods.
(B) The leg from the Americas to Europe, carrying plantation products to market.
(C) The leg from Africa to the Americas, carrying enslaved people to work plantations.
(D) Trade conducted entirely within a single colony's borders.
items.stem: This 1830 image shows a West Indies sugar plantation worked by enslaved laborers. In the triangular trade, plantation products such as sugar represented which leg of the system?

stimulus.image_caption: Hand-colored engraving by Paolo Fumagalli, 1830, showing a West Indies sugar plantation with enslaved workers, plantation buildings, and cane fields.

items.explanation: Havana was the gathering point of Spain's Atlantic system: treasure fleets assembled there carrying American silver and colonial products to Spain. The crowded harbor shows a port city whose whole economy served the flow of American wealth to Europe under Spanish control.
items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — Potosi silver 'flowed into European treasuries and the world economy'; Spain 'built an empire on forced labor... and on silver'

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Havana was Spanish; the English slave trade operated under a different flag and system.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the French fur trade centered on Canada and the interior, not Havana.
option_explanations.C: Right — Havana funneled American silver and goods to Europe for Spain.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Navigation Acts governed English colonies, not Spanish Cuba.

options: (A) The English triangular trade in enslaved Africans.
(B) The French fur trade with Native allies in Canada and the Great Lakes region.
(C) The movement of American silver and goods through Spanish ports to Europe.
(D) English colonial commerce regulated under the Navigation Acts of the 1660s.
items.stem: This 1765 engraving shows the harbor of Havana, Cuba, crowded with sailing ships. As a major Spanish Atlantic port, Havana's importance rested on its role in which system?

stimulus.image_caption: 'A view of the harbour and city of the Havana,' drawn by Elias Durnford and engraved by Pierre Charles Canot, 1765: sailing ships crowded in the harbor.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1765 engraving; pre-1930, public domain (Library of Congress)

items.explanation: Forcing trade through specific ports concentrated commerce there: colonial tobacco, sugar, and rice flowed out through port cities while English manufactured goods flowed in. Merchants in those ports grew rich handling both directions — the review notes colonial merchants prospering on imported English goods.
items.fact_source: u2.md §Key terms — Navigation Acts: 'requiring colonial trade to use English ships and pass through English ports'; u2.md §The story — 'merchants to grow rich on imported English goods'

option_explanations.A: Right — the Acts funneled trade through ports, concentrating wealth there.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the Acts redirected trade; they did not ban it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the laws favored ports, not inland towns.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the Acts restricted trade to English channels; they did not open it to all nations.

options: (A) Ports grew as bottlenecks for colonial exports and English imports, enriching merchants.
(B) Port cities withered and declined because the Navigation Acts banned nearly all colonial trade with anyone.
(C) Only inland towns benefited from the new trade rules.
(D) Colonial ports began trading freely with every nation.
items.stem: The Navigation Acts required colonial goods to pass through English ports carried on English ships. What was the most likely effect of these laws on Atlantic port cities?

items.explanation: The chain runs from the plantation: rice and tobacco needed large labor forces, enslaved labor filled that need, and the transatlantic slave trade supplied the workers. Plantation demand is what made the Middle Passage crossing — and the Africa-to-Americas leg — so massive.
items.fact_source: u2.md §The story — 'The Lower South — South Carolina's rice plantations... by the early 1700s enslaved people outnumbered free whites in South Carolina'; u2.md §Key terms — Triangular trade; Middle Passage

option_explanations.A: Wrong — plantations grew crops; manufactured goods came from Europe.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — rice and tobacco were American plantation crops, not African ones.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — plantation colonies were deeply embedded in Atlantic commerce.
option_explanations.D: Right — labor demand on plantations drove the slave-trade leg from Africa.

options: (A) Plantations manufactured the finished goods that Europe then shipped to Africa for trade.
(B) Rice and tobacco were grown on plantations in Africa and shipped directly to Europe.
(C) Plantation colonies refused to take part in Atlantic commerce.
(D) Planters' demand for workers drove the Africa-to-Americas leg across the Middle Passage.
items.stem: South Carolina's rice plantations and the Chesapeake's tobacco plantations ran on enslaved labor — by the early 1700s, enslaved people outnumbered free whites in South Carolina. Which statement best connects these plantation economies to the triangular trade?

items.explanation: The review frames the period as a tension: mercantilist law claimed colonial trade for England, while salutary neglect let assemblies and merchants operate freely. That unresolved tension — control on paper, autonomy in practice — is exactly what would snap when Britain later enforced its laws strictly.
items.fact_source: u2.md §What the exam tests here — 'Imperial control vs. colonial autonomy — Navigation Acts and the Dominion on one side, salutary neglect and powerful assemblies on the other; the tension is the bridge into Period 3'

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the Navigation Acts explicitly subordinated colonial trade to England.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — colonists grew more English in taste and merchants grew rich on imported English goods.
option_explanations.C: Right — mercantilist control versus colonial autonomy is the period's central imperial tension.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — mercantilist policy continued; enforcement, not the doctrine, is what changed.

options: (A) Mercantilism gave the colonies complete economic independence from England in all matters of trade and taxation.
(B) The colonies rejected English goods throughout the entire colonial period as a matter of policy.
(C) Mercantilist policies treated colonies as England's economic resources, creating tension with colonial autonomy.
(D) England abandoned mercantilism before 1700.
items.stem: Which argument about mercantilism and the British colonies is best supported by the evidence of this period?
